description: We're a team of three taking on the "Be an Earth System Trend Detective" challenge. We want to dig into NASA Earth data, find real trends, and explain them in a clear, simple way. Our team brings data analysis, machine learning and backend skills, plus a simple interface to show the results.
summary:
Trend Detective is a web app that turns NASA Earth data into a clear, trustworthy answer to one question: is it really changing?

Users pick one of 21 cities on every inhabited continent, either from a list or on a map, and one of 10 measures, each explained in plain words: temperature, precipitation, air humidity, wind, vegetation greenness, soil moisture, evaporation and snow. The app then shows 24 years of data (2001–2024) from NASA POWER (MERRA-2), AppEEARS (MODIS) and Giovanni (GLDAS) as a yearly chart with a trend line. A short answer card says whether the measure is rising or falling, how fast and how much since 2001.

Each trend is checked with two tests, a linear t-test and Mann-Kendall, and is marked as trustworthy only when both agree. Compare places two cities on one chart to show that one measure can move in opposite directions in different regions. Detective suggests the clearest findings after two quick questions, and "Explain this chart" gives a short plain-English explanation built only from verified numbers.

The app covers every step of the challenge in a form that high school and college students can use without a statistics background.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Trend Detective helps anyone answer one question about our planet: is it really changing? A user picks one of 21 capital cities (from a list or by tapping a world map) and one of 10 measures: mean, maximum and minimum temperature, precipitation, air humidity, wind speed, vegetation greenness (NDVI), soil moisture, evaporation and snow depth. Every measure is explained in one plain line.

The app instantly shows:

- An answer card: Rising, Falling or No clear trend, one plain sentence ("Beijing got greener from 2001 to 2024"), the total change since 2001, the speed per 10 years, and "Can we trust it? Yes/Not sure".

- A chart of yearly averages with a dashed trend line, plus a monthly view that shows the seasonal cycle.

- "Show the statistics": linear slope, 95% confidence interval, t-test p-value, Mann-Kendall p-value, Kendall's tau and Sen's slope.

- "Explain this chart": a 2–4 sentence plain-English explanation for students.

Compare puts two cities on one chart to show that one measure can move in opposite directions in different regions. Detective asks two questions (what interests you, what kind of place) and returns the three clearest findings. How it works explains the measures, the method and the data sources.

HOW IT WORKS

Data: 2001–2024 monthly values for 21 cities, taken from NASA POWER (MERRA-2), AppEEARS (MODIS Terra MOD13A3) and Giovanni (GLDAS Noah 2.1) with our NASA Earthdata login. We processed and merged them in Jupyter notebooks into two compact files that load instantly.

Method: monthly values are averaged by year to remove the seasonal cycle. A linear regression gives the speed of change per decade and its 95% confidence interval. Significance is tested with a linear t-test and the Mann-Kendall test, and a trend is called trustworthy only when both have p < 0.05. "No clear trend" is shown as a valid result, not a failure.

AI explanations: a language model (via OpenRouter) receives only our verified numbers. Every number in its answer is checked against the data. Any unknown number, link or formatting, or a timeout, falls back to a template explanation built from the same numbers, so users always get a correct answer.

WHY 21 CITIES — AND HOW IT SCALES

Getting the data was the slowest part of the project. Each source has its own process: some requests needed to be submitted and then waited in a processing queue (often pending for a long time during the hackathon weekend), and only then could the results be downloaded and converted. Doing this for every city in the world was not possible within the challenge time. So we chose 21 capital cities that together cover every inhabited continent and every major climate type: deserts, tropics, the cold north, temperate zones and Central Asia.

The 21 cities are a data limit, not a design limit. Nothing in the app is built for these specific cities: every page, chart, test and explanation works the same way for any location that has the same monthly data. Adding a city means running the same analysis on its data. Connected to a fast NASA data API, Trend Detective could fetch and analyze any point on Earth on demand and become a fully global tool.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

Python 3.12, FastAPI, Pydantic, Jinja2 templates, Chart.js, plain HTML/CSS/JavaScript, the Inter font (self-hosted), pytest (over 120 automated tests), ruff, GitHub Actions for continuous integration, and Render for hosting. Data work: Jupyter notebooks, pandas, NASA POWER, AppEEARS and Giovanni. We used AI coding assistants under our direction for parts of the implementation; all design decisions, data processing and verification were done by our team.

BENEFITS

- No statistics background needed: one word, one sentence and three numbers answer the question.

- Honest: two independent tests protect against trends that are only random noise.

- Transparent: experts can open every statistic behind each answer.

- Fast and reliable: all pages load in under a second, on desktop and mobile, in light and dark mode.

INTENDED IMPACT

Trend Detective is built for high school and college classrooms and for curious adults. It turns NASA data into a hands-on lesson in how scientists separate a real trend from natural ups and downs, and why the same process can push a measure up in one place and down in another.

CREATIVITY

- A "detective" experience: users ask a question, collect evidence and get a verdict they can trust.

- A world map whose dots change color with the trend of the selected measure.

- A guided Detective mode for users who don't know where to start.

- AI explanations that are fact-checked against the data before they are shown.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Audience: simple English, short sentences, terms explained the first time they appear.

- Scientific validity: a 24-year period long enough for trend tests, removal of the seasonal cycle, two tests instead of one, and the same numbers in the chart, the card and the explanation.

- Coverage vs. time: with slow data access, we chose 21 well-spread cities over a few regions, and kept the app location-independent so it can grow.

- Clarity: one main answer per screen, consistent colors (blue = rising, orange = falling, gray = no clear trend), with arrows and words so color is never the only signal.

- Accessibility: keyboard navigation, good contrast and readable charts.

- Reliability: prepared data, automatic tests and safe fallbacks for every external service.

Source code: https://github.com/rmarufs/earth-trend-detective
